title:
A data investigation of how the American middle-class
      life stopped being affordable,
      and what to do about it.
text:
Your browser does not support the video tag. Please

 Bob Dylan
 The Times They Are A-Changin'
 1965
 

 
 
 In 1960, a working American could afford a home,
 raise a family, and retire with dignity
 on a single income.
 
 
 Today, that same life costs more
 than the median household earns.
 
 
 
 This is not a personal failure.
 It is a structural one.
 
 
 

 
 scroll
 
 
 
 

 

 
 NBC News archive · Independent documentary
 





  

    
      
      The Asset Contract
      
    

    
      A data investigation of how the American middle-class
      life stopped being affordable,
      and what to do about it.
    

    
      Built from sixty-five years of federal economic data,
      thirteen primary sources, and the voices of Americans
      who lived through the shift. Roughly 45 minutes to read
      end-to-end. Each chapter stands alone.
    

    

    
      The journey:
      
        
          I
          The Architecture
          how the asset contract was built, 1934–1977
        
        
          II
          The Dream Index
          the measurement that tracks unaffordability
        
        
          III
          The Break
          when wages stopped tracking productivity, 1973
        
        
          IV
          What Worked, For Whom
          women and immigrants inside the asset economy
        
        
          V
          Five Americas
          five communities, five mechanisms
        
        
          VI
          The Asset Gap
          why income gains have not closed the racial wealth gap
        
        
          VII
          Human Cost
          delayed marriage, falling fertility, shortened lives
        
        
          VIII
          Find Yourself
          your life on the Dream Index
        
        
          IX
          The Reckoning
          recommendations and the action plan
        
      
    

    

    
      Inspired by Studs Terkel's
      Working, Bill Moyers's Two American
      Families, Elizabeth Warren's Two-Income Trap,
      and Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First
      Century. Data from FRED, the Kaiser Family Foundation,
      the National Center for Education Statistics, the National
      Historical Geographic Information System, the Bureau of
      Labor Statistics, the Federal Housing Finance Agency,
      and the Survey of Consumer Finances.
    

    
      Scroll to begin
      
        
      
    

  





 
 
 
 
 The Architecture
 
 The Architecture
 What was built, deliberately

 
   Before the numbers, the policies. This chapter is a
   walk through the legislative architecture that built
   the postwar American middle class, and the laws that
   later disassembled it. The Dream Index, the measurement
   that tracks what those policies produced, arrives in
   the next chapter.
 

 The GI Bill sent eight million veterans to college on
 the federal government's account. The FHA drove
 homeownership from 44% in 1940 to 62% by 1960. Union
 membership reached 35% of the workforce. For the people
 inside this architecture, it worked.

 But the architecture had exclusions built in. The FHA's
 own manuals recommended against insuring mortgages in
 racially mixed neighborhoods. Black veterans found the GI
 Bill administered locally by the same people who enforced
 segregation. The Dream was always rationed.

 
 "In 1960, a median household spent 44 cents of every
 earned dollar on the full basket of middle-class life.
 That 44 cents would become $1.20 by 2024."
 
 

 
 
 
 Levittown, Pennsylvania, late 1950s. Built for returning
 veterans using GI Bill financing and FHA-insured mortgages
 the postwar architecture of mass homeownership.
 Wikimedia Commons. Public domain.
 
 
 





 
 Figure 1, The Architecture, in Decisions
 The asset contract was built between 1934 and 1977, then dismantled in the decades that followed.
 Twenty federal policy actions, plotted on a
 single timeline. The eleven dots above the ribbon are the
 laws that built the middle-class architecture, the GI Bill,
 Social Security, Medicare, the Community Reinvestment Act.
 The nine dots below are the laws that dismantled it,
 beginning with the 1978 enactment of the 401(k) and
 accelerating through the 1980s tax cuts and the 1999 repeal
 of Glass-Steagall. The pivot is visible in the structure of
 the chart itself.
 
 
 
 
 








 
 
 
 

 
 1945, 1973
 The Promise
 
 For thirty years, America built a specific kind of
 future for its working people. A house. A single
 income that covered it. Healthcare that came with
 the job. A degree the next generation could afford.
 
 
 These are the voices of Americans who lived inside
 that promise, before the wages stopped tracking
 productivity, before the contract changed.
 
 
 
 Studs Terkel, "Working Americans on Home Ownership"
, 1971. Clip: 1:28–1:55.
 
 





 
 What is the Dream Index?
 How do you put a number on a broken promise?

 The Dream Index measures the annual cost of a canonical
 middle-class American life, a median home mortgage, family
 health insurance, one year of public college tuition,
 center-based childcare, vehicle ownership and operation,
 and a family's food budget, expressed as a fraction of
 median household income.

 When the index reads 0.44, as it did in 1960, the basket
 consumed 44 cents of every dollar the median household earned.
 When it reads 1.19, as it does in 2024, the basket costs 19%
 more than the median household earns in an entire year. All
 values are expressed in real 2024 dollars, adjusted for
 inflation using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban
 Consumers (CPI-U).

 The index does not measure subjective wellbeing or
 lifestyle preferences. It measures a single arithmetic fact:
 can the median American household afford what was once
 considered a standard American life?
 











 
 Figure 2, The Dream Index
 The American Dream Became Unaffordable in 2011
 

 

 

 
 01 · The frame
 Two trajectories, one country
 For sixty-five years, two numbers measured
 the same idea: what an American household earned,
 and what an American life cost.
 The first is median household income, adjusted
 for inflation. The second is the Dream Basket 
 a canonical middle-class life: housing, healthcare,
 education, childcare, transportation, and food.
 For half a century, these two lines were inseparable.
 Then they weren't.
 

 
 02 · What households earned
 Income rose, but slowly
 In real 2024 dollars, the typical American
 household earned $41,348 in 1960. By 2024, it
 earned $83,753.
 A doubling, but a doubling spread across
 sixty-four years. Roughly 1.1% real growth
 per year, on average. Less in the most recent
 three decades.
 

 
 03 · What a life cost
 The basket rose faster
 The Dream Basket cost $18,213 in 1960. By 2024
 it cost $100,083, a 5.5x increase in real terms.
 Housing, healthcare, education, and childcare
 all rose faster than wages. Consumer goods got
 cheaper. The basket was reshaped by what was
 possible to import (clothing, electronics) and
 what was not (housing, the human time of
 teachers, doctors, and child caregivers).
 

 
 04 · Four chapters
 The story has four periods
 Postwar Promise (1960–1973):
 the basket cost less than half of household income.
 Erosion (1973–2007):
 wages decoupled from productivity. The gap closed.
 Crisis (2008–2011):
 the financial collapse accelerated what was
 already happening.
 Rate floor and after (2012–today):
 cheap mortgages briefly disguised the problem.
 When rates rose in 2022, the gap reopened.
 

 
 05 · The crossing
 In 2011, the lines crossed
 For the first time in measurable American
 history, the cost of a canonical middle-class life
 exceeded what the typical household earned.
 Basket: $70,372. Income: $69,804.
 Gap: $568.
 $568 is approximately three months of childcare
 for one child, or 60% of community college tuition
 for a year. A small number that crossed a
 meaningful line.
 

 
 06 · The gap widens
 And then it kept widening
 The rust-colored area is the gap. Every year
 the basket cost more than the median household
 earned, by an amount visible on the chart.
 By 2024, the gap was $16,330, equivalent to
 one full year of in-state college tuition, or
 six months of family health insurance premiums.
 Or roughly four months of rent for a median
 two-bedroom apartment in any American metro.
 

 
 07 · What it sounded like
 The same story, in three voices
 
 "We were doing okay. A house, a car, a steady
 job. That was a life."
 
 Steel worker, Pittsburgh, 1965
 
 
 
 "The plant kept producing. My paycheck stopped
 growing. I didn't understand why."
 
 UAW assembler, Flint, 1979
 
 
 
 "We did everything right. Two degrees. Two jobs.
 And we still can't buy the house my parents had."
 
 Teacher, Cleveland, 2012
 
 
 

 
 08 · The argument
 This is not a personal failure
 The crossing happened to everyone at once.
 It is not a story of individual choices, individual
 failures, or individual generations.
 The basket and the income are calculated
 identically for every American household. The
 crossing is the structural fact this project
 exists to document.
 The rest of this site explains how it happened 
 which mechanisms broke first, who was protected,
 who was not, and what it costs to live in a country
 where the arithmetic of a middle-class life no
 longer works.
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 





 
 Figure 3, The Bifurcation
 What got cheaper. What got more expensive.
 Consumer goods collapsed in real price.
 The essentials for building a life exploded. America made
 consumption affordable and existence expensive.
 
 
 
 





 
 Figure 4, Basket composition
 The basket didn't just grow, its shape changed.
 Healthcare consumed about 5% of the dream
 basket in 1960. By 2024 it consumes 25%. Housing's share
 fell from two-thirds to one-quarter, not because housing
 got cheap but because everything else expanded around it.
 
 
 
 








 
 
 
 

 
 1973, 1984
 The Break
 
 In 1973, wages stopped tracking productivity.
 On September 19, 1977, Black Monday, Youngstown
 Sheet and Tube closed, laying off 5,000 workers.
 
 
 It was not an anomaly. It was the beginning of a
 pattern that would hollow out manufacturing America
 over the next fifty years.
 
 
 
 "Aftermath of the 1977 Youngstown Steel Mill Closure", YouTube
 
 





 
 
 
 
 The Mechanism
 
 The Mechanism
 When labor stopped being rewarded

 
   Union membership began its long decline from 35% toward
   10%. Trade policy opened manufacturing to global
   competition. Corporate governance shifted toward
   shareholder returns. Each change redirected productivity
   gains away from workers and toward capital.
 

 The figure below makes this concrete. Nonfarm business
 output per hour, a standard measure of economic productivity,
 is indexed alongside real manufacturing wages, both set to
 100 in 1960. Until 1973 the lines move together, confirming
 that workers were capturing the gains of the economy they
 built. After 1973, they do not. The gap between what the
 economy produced and what workers were paid has widened
 every decade since.

 The shaded area beneath the divergence is not abstract:
 it represents wages that were earned by the economy but not
 distributed to the workers who generated them. The figure
 also shows a third line, what wages would be today if they
 had tracked productivity since 1973. The distance between
 that hypothetical line and actual wages is the arithmetic
 of the asset contract.

 
 "If wages had tracked productivity since 1973, the median
 American worker would earn approximately $20 more
 per hour today."
 
 

 
 
 
 U.S. Steel Lorain Works, 1975.
 Union membership peaked at 35% of the workforce in the
 postwar years; by 2024 it had fallen below 10%.
 Wikimedia Commons. Public domain.
 
 
 





 
 Figure 5, Wages vs. Productivity
 Wages vs. Productivity, 1960–2024
 Both indexed to 100 in 1960. The lines track
 together through the postwar period, then separate in 1973.
 The gap is the engine of the asset contract.
 
 
 
 





 
 Figure 6, Hours of work
 What the basket costs in weeks of full-time work.
 An alternative way to read the divergence:
 instead of inflation-adjusted dollars, count weeks of
 median-wage work to cover one year of each component, in
 1960 vs. 2024. Healthcare went from about a week of work
 to roughly four months. The total basket tripled.
 
 
 
 





 
 Figure 7, Where the gains went
 The productivity gains went to the top 1%
 If wages didn't capture the productivity
 gains since 1973, who did? The Federal Reserve's
 Distributional Financial Accounts answer the question for
 1989 onward: the top 1% expanded its share of US household
 wealth from 22.9% to 31.2%. The bottom 50% shrank from
 3.5% to 2.5%.
 
 
 
 









 

 
 What Worked, and For Whom
 The contract did not fail everyone equally

 The asset contract created genuine winners alongside
 genuine losers. Two groups illustrate what success
 looked like, and what enabled it.

 Women's entry into the professional workforce is one
 of the most consequential economic transformations of
 the 20th century. Women's labor force participation
 rose from 38% in 1960 to 58% today. Women now earn the
 majority of college degrees. The gender wage gap has
 narrowed substantially. These are real gains, not
 statistical artifacts, not incomplete progress dressed
 as completion, but measurable improvements in access,
 opportunity, and economic independence.
 

 
 
 
 J. Howard Miller, We Can Do It!, 1942.
 Westinghouse Electric & Manufacturing Company.
 Wikimedia Commons (NARA restoration). Public domain.
 
 

 
 Immigrants who arrived in the United States before
 2000 and purchased homes have, in many cases,
 accumulated wealth comparable to or exceeding
 native-born Americans of similar education. The
 first-generation story of arrival, labor, and
 eventual stability is real and documented. In
 communities across America, it happened.

 
 "The asset contract is not broken for everyone.
 It is broken for those who arrived after the
 prices changed."
 

 Both stories share a structural feature: timing.
 Women who entered professional careers in the 1970s
 and 1980s, when credential returns were rising and
 housing was still affordable, built wealth. Immigrants
 who arrived before 2000 and bought homes at
 pre-crossing prices built wealth. The mechanism that
 rewarded them is the same mechanism that now
 forecloses the same path to those who come after.

 This is not an argument against women's advancement
 or immigrant success. It is an argument about
 structure. The asset contract produced winners. The
 question this project asks is whether those wins are
 reproducible, and what the data says is that they
 are not, at current entry prices, without fundamental
 structural change.
 

 





 
 Figure 8, Women and the Dream
 Women entered the economy. The basket helped require it.
 Women's labor force participation rose
 from 38% to 58% between 1960 and 2024, one of the most
 significant economic transformations in American history.
 The right panel shows this shift alongside the Dream
 Index. Both lines rise. Their relationship is not a
 coincidence or a contradiction. It is the asset contract
 adapting.
 
 
 
 





 
 Figure 9, Immigrant Economic Trajectories
 The same dream. Different entry prices.
 Immigrant households by decade of arrival,
 measured in 2024. Those who arrived before 2000 achieved
 incomes above the national median and homeownership rates
 approaching national norms. Those who arrived after 2010
 face a basket that costs $100,083 against a median
 immigrant household income of roughly $60,000. Not
 because of different effort, because of different
 entry prices.
 
 
 
 








 
 
 
 

 
 Five Places, One Economy
 Five Americas
 
 The national data tells one story. Five American
 communities tell five others, each shaped by a
 different mechanism of the same structural shift.
 
 
 
 SHARECROP: Delta Cotton, YouTube (2023)
 
 





 

 Five Americas, Five Mechanisms
 Why these five communities

 
   The national Dream Index is a single number. The country
   is not. To average a contract that worked for some and
   never reached others is to describe nothing accurately.
 

 This chapter looks at five specific American
 communities. They are not random examples. Together they
 form a typology of asset contract failure, each one
 representing a structurally distinct way the postwar
 economic deal either never extended, was withdrawn, was
 made obsolete, or worked as designed and still broke.

 The Mississippi Delta shows the
 contract deliberately denied. Pine Ridge
 shows it never extended. Coal Country
 shows it extended and then abandoned when the underlying
 asset ran out. The Rust Belt shows it
 extended and then made obsolete by globalization. The
 Bay Area and NYC show what happens when
 the contract works exactly as designed, and locally breaks
 anyway.

 Five communities. Five mechanisms. One contract, five
 different ways of failing.

 





 
   Five Americas, Mapped
   The atlas
   
     Five markers. Five mechanisms. Click any community to
     read its full story, the photo, the data, the quotes,
     the trajectories across six decades.
   
 

 





 
 Figure 12, Community Abandonment
 What a manufacturing town actually lost
 The Rust Belt panel in Figure 11 shows
 Mahoning County's income trajectory as a line. This figure
 shows what that line is made of, jobs that existed and
 then did not. Each square is 1% of the 1960 manufacturing
 workforce, roughly 1,100 jobs. Watch the filled squares
 disappear decade by decade. By 2020, only 11 of every 100
 manufacturing jobs that existed in 1960 remain.
 
 
 
 





 
   The Asset Gap
   How the gap is made.
 

 
   

     
       Act I, The income gap
       Black households earn 64¢ for every $1 white
       households earn.
       64¢
       This gap has narrowed. In 1967 the ratio was
       55¢. Six decades later it sits at 64¢, a 9-cent
       gain across two generations.
       Income narrows when wages rise. Wages have
       risen, slowly, unevenly, but they have risen. The
       labor market, for all its faults, partially
       responded.
     

     
       Act II, The wealth gap
       But Black households own 12¢ for every $1 of
       wealth white households own.
       12¢
       In 1989 the ratio was 9¢. Today it is 12¢.
       Three cents in 33 years. The wealth gap has barely
       moved while the income gap has slowly narrowed.
       This is the question the chapter exists to
       answer: why?
     

     
       Act III, The mechanism
       Imagine two households in 1989. Identical in
       every way except one thing.
       Both earn the same income. Both save 8% of it.
       Both invest in assets that return 6% a year.
       The only difference is their starting balance.
       The median white household held $100,000 in
       assets. The median Black household held $9,300.
       This is not because of effort. It is because of
       sixty prior years of denied access to the asset
       contract, the FHA mortgages, the GI Bill, the
       union pensions, the suburbs.
     

     
       Act IV, Compounding
       Project them forward 35 years.
       Same savings rate. Same return. Same effort.
       The trajectories diverge, not because one earned
       more, but because compound interest pays a return
       on what you already own.
       The absolute gap widens with every year.
       Compounding does not close gaps. It amplifies
       them.
     

     
       Act V, Today
       This is the wealth gap today.
       The median white household has roughly
       $285,000 in net worth. The median Black household
       has roughly $44,000.
       The gap is not made by who earned more this
       year. It is made by who was allowed to buy assets
       sixty years ago, and who has therefore been
       compounding ever since.
       This is the asset contract's central trick. It
       rewards what you already own.
     

   

   
     
   
 





 
 Figure 14, Compound the Difference
 The asset your parents bought outearned their labor
 For most American homeowners, the house
 they bought decades ago has appreciated more than they
 earned from working. Enter the year and city to see
 your family's compound.
 
 
 
 
 








 
 
 
 

 
 2000, 2024
 What It Cost
 
 The economic pressure did not stay in balance sheets.
 It showed up in bedrooms, birth certificates,
 and obituaries.
 
 
 
 "A Thunder-Being Nation: The Oglala Lakota of Pine Ridge", YouTube
 
 





 

   The Consequences
   Economic distress does not stay in
   financial statements.

   When households cannot
   afford the basket of basic life, they restructure the
   shape of their lives. They delay marriage because
   forming a household requires two incomes and a deposit
   they cannot save. They have fewer children than they
   say they want because childcare costs more than rent in
   most American cities. They move back in with parents
   because renting alone consumes more than 30% of
   take-home income. And in communities where economic
   abandonment is most complete, they die younger.

   The four indicators below, median age at first
   marriage, total fertility rate, share of adults in
   multigenerational households, life expectancy at
   birth, are not separate phenomena. They are four
   measurements of the same underlying pressure. Each has
   moved in the direction the Dream Index would predict.
   Each accelerated after 2000, when the index began its
   final climb toward 1.0.

   This is what the data looks like when you measure
   it not in dollars, but in years of life and choices
   foreclosed.

 





 
 Figure 16, Way of Life
 What Americans gave up to keep paying
 Marriage age, fertility, multigenerational
 households, and life expectancy since 1960. Each one tracks
 the pressure of the rising Dream Index. Use the buttons
 above the chart to switch between the four metrics.
 
 
 
 








 
 Figure 17, Your Life on the Dream Index
 Find yourself in the Dream Index
 Pick your generation, education, and community.
 The basket cost stays the same, your income changes, and the
 Dream Index recomputes for a household like yours.
 
 
 
 
 








 
 
 
 

 
 April 3, 1968
 The Reckoning
 
 The asset contract was not destiny. It was decided.
 The specific decisions that created it are documented.
 They can be decided differently.
 
 
 
 Martin Luther King Jr., Mason Temple, Memphis, April 3, 1968.
 The night before his assassination, in support of the
 sanitation workers' strike.
 
 





 

   The Reckoning
   Seven findings. One contract to rewrite.

   The evidence assembled across
   this project points to a single structural shift: the
   American economy transitioned, between roughly 1973 and
   2011, from a system that delivered middle-class life
   through wages to one that requires asset ownership,
   credentialed employment, or inherited capital.

   The seven memos that follow are not separate
   arguments. They are seven different measurements of the
   same underlying change, and seven concrete
   interventions, each tied to one mechanism documented in
   the preceding chapters. Each could be delivered to a
   working policymaker today.

   
     The architecture of the Dream was built through
     specific decisions. Rebuilding it requires specific
     decisions, not generic growth, but targeted structural
     repair.
   

 






 
   The Reckoning
   Seven policy memos.
   
     The data analysis ends here. What follows is the case
     it makes, seven concrete policy interventions, each
     addressing one mechanism documented in the preceding
     chapters. Each memo is a brief that could be delivered
     to a working policymaker today.
   
 

 
   
 






 
 Figure 19, Your Action Plan
 What this means for you, specifically
 The findings of this project, applied to
 your household. Enter what you know. The engine produces a
 personalized action plan across the five domains the project
 documents, housing, healthcare, childcare, education, and
 asset allocation. Every recommendation is traceable to project
 findings. No data leaves your browser.
 
 
 
 
 








 
 
 
 Methodology
 
 
 Technical Documentation
 Methodology & Data
 

 The Dream Index measures
 the cost of housing, healthcare, education, childcare,
 transportation, and food as a multiple of median household
 income. All values in real 2024 dollars using CPI-U as
 the deflator. Primary healthcare measure uses the full
 KFF family premium (crosses 1.0 in 2011). Conservative
 lower bound uses household exposure only (crosses 2022).

 Data sources:
 FRED (38 series), KFF Employer Health Benefits Survey
 (1999–2024), NCES Digest Table 330.10 (1963+), NHGIS
 county-level census data (1960–2020), CDC NCHS life
 expectancy and birth rates, BLS Consumer Price Indices.

 Five places:
 Counties aggregated to place level using population-weighted
 averages. Pine Ridge merges FIPS 46-102 and 46-113 as one
 continuous series. All income comparisons use nominal
 values divided by national nominal median, the ratio
 cancels inflation, no deflation required.

 
 Full methodology, sensitivity analyses, and data files:
 dream_index_metadata.json

 teachers, doctors, and child caregivers).
 

 
 04 · Four chapters
 The story has four periods
 Postwar Promise (1960–1973):
 the basket cost less than half of household income.
 Erosion (1973–2007):
 wages decoupled from productivity. The gap closed.
 Crisis (2008–2011):
 the financial collapse accelerated what was
 already happening.
 Rate floor and after (2012–today):
 cheap mortgages briefly disguised the problem.
 When rates rose in 2022, the gap reopened.
 

 
 05 · The crossing
 In 2011, the lines crossed
 For the first time in measurable American
 history, the cost of a canonical middle-class life
 exceeded what the typical household earned.
 Basket: $70,372. Income: $69,804.
 Gap: $568.
 $568 is approximately three months of childcare
 for one child, or 60% of community college tuition
 for a year. A small number that crossed a
 meaningful line.
 

 
 06 · The gap widens
 And then it kept widening
 The rust-colored area is the gap. Every year
 the basket cost more than the median household
 earned, by an amount visible on the chart.
 By 2024, the gap was $16,330, equivalent to
 one full year of in-state college tuition, or
 six months of family health insurance premiums.
 Or roughly four months of rent for a median
 two-bedroom apartment in any American metro.
 

 
 07 · What it sounded like
 The same story, in three voices
 
 "We were doing okay. A house, a car, a steady
 job. That was a life."
 
 Steel worker, Pittsburgh, 1965
 
 
 
 "The plant kept producing. My paycheck stopped
 growing. I didn't understand why."
 
 UAW assembler, Flint, 1979
 
 
 
 "We did everything right. Two degrees. Two jobs.
 And we still can't buy the house my parents had."
 
 Teacher, Cleveland, 2012
 
 
 

 
 08 · The argument
 This is not a personal failure
 The crossing happened to everyone at once.
 It is not a story of individual choices, individual
 failures, or individual generations.
 The basket and the income are calculated
 identically for every American household. The
 crossing is the structural fact this project
 exists to document.
 The rest of this site explains how it happened 
 which mechanisms broke first, who was protected,
 who was not, and what it costs to live in a country
 where the arithmetic of a middle-class life no
 longer works.
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 





 
 Figure 3, The Bifurcation
 What got cheaper. What got more expensive.
 Consumer goods collapsed in real price.
 The essentials for building a life exploded. America made
 consumption affordable and existence expensive.
 
 
 
 





 
 Figure 4, Basket composition
 The basket didn't just grow, its shape changed.
 Healthcare consumed about 5% of the dream
 basket in 1960. By 2024 it consumes 25%. Housing's share
 fell from two-thirds to one-quarter, not because housing
 got cheap but because everything else expanded around it.
 
 
 
 








 
 
 
 

 
 1973, 1984
 The Break
 
 In 1973, wages stopped tracking productivity.
 On September 19, 1977, Black Monday, Youngstown
 Sheet and Tube closed, laying off 5,000 workers.
 
 
 It was not an anomaly. It was the beginning of a
 pattern that would hollow out manufacturing America
 over the next fifty years.
 
 
 
 "Aftermath of the 1977 Youngstown Steel Mill Closure", YouTube
 
 





 
 
 
 
 The Mechanism
 
 When labor stopped being rewarded

 Union membership began its long decline from 35% toward
 10%. Trade policy opened manufacturing to global competition.
 Corporate governance shifted toward shareholder returns.
 Each change redirected productivity gains away from workers
 and toward capital.

 
 "If wages had tracked productivity since 1973, the median
 American worker would earn approximately $20 more
 per hour today."
 
 

 
 
 
 U.S. Steel Lorain Works, 1975.
 Union membership peaked at 35% of the workforce in the
 postwar years; by 2024 it had fallen below 10%.
 Wikimedia Commons. Public domain.
 
 

 
 The figure below makes this concrete. Nonfarm business
 output per hour, a standard measure of economic productivity
, is indexed alongside real manufacturing wages, both set to
 100 in 1960. Until 1973 the lines move together, confirming
 that workers were capturing the gains of the economy they
 built. After 1973, they do not. The gap between what the
 economy produced and what workers were paid has widened every
 decade since. The shaded area beneath the divergence is not
 abstract: it represents wages that were earned by the economy
 but not distributed to the workers who generated them. The
 figure also shows a third line, what wages would be today
 if they had tracked productivity since 1973. The distance
 between that hypothetical line and actual wages is the
 arithmetic of the asset contract.

 
 Coal Country, McDowell County, WV
 Extraction economy abandoned after the asset ran out
 McDowell County peaked in the 1950s with 100,000 people
 and wages above the national median. When the coal ran out
 and strip mining mechanized extraction, nothing replaced
 it. Today: 18,000 residents. Median income 47% of national.
 

 
 Rust Belt, Youngstown, OH / Janesville, WI
 Manufacturing made disposable by globalization
 Youngstown's Black Monday in 1977. Janesville's GM
 closure in 2008. The same story, thirty years apart.
 The local Dream Index collapsed in a single year both times.

 Figure 7, Where the gains went
 The productivity gains went to the top 1%
 If wages didn't capture the productivity
 gains since 1973, who did? The Federal Reserve's
 Distributional Financial Accounts answer the question for
 1989 onward: the top 1% expanded its share of US household
 wealth from 22.9% to 31.2%. The bottom 50% shrank from
 3.5% to 2.5%.
 
 
 
 









 

 
 What Worked, and For Whom
 The contract did not fail everyone equally

 The asset contract created genuine winners alongside
 genuine losers. Two groups illustrate what success
 looked like, and what enabled it.

 Women's entry into the professional workforce is one
 of the most consequential economic transformations of
 the 20th century. Women's labor force participation
 rose from 38% in 1960 to 58% today. Women now earn the
 majority of college degrees. The gender wage gap has
 narrowed substantially. These are real gains, not
 statistical artifacts, not incomplete progress dressed
 as completion, but measurable improvements in access,
 opportunity, and economic independence.
 

 
 
 
 J. Howard Miller, We Can Do It!, 1942.
 Westinghouse Electric & Manufacturing Company.
 Wikimedia Commons (NARA restoration). Public domain.
 
 

 
 Immigrants who arrived in the United States before
 2000 and purchased homes have, in many cases,
 accumulated wealth comparable to or exceeding
 native-born Americans of similar education. The
 first-generation story of arrival, labor, and
 eventual stability is real and documented. In
 communities across America, it happened.

 
 "The asset contract is not broken for everyone.
 It is broken for those who arrived after the
 prices changed."
 

 Both stories share a structural feature: timing.
 Women who entered professional careers in the 1970s
 and 1980s, when credential returns were rising and
 housing was still affordable, built wealth. Immigrants
 who arrived before 2000 and bought homes at
 pre-crossing prices built wealth. The mechanism that
 rewarded them is the same mechanism that now
 forecloses the same path to those who come after.

 This is not an argument against women's advancement
 or immigrant success. It is an argument about
 structure. The asset contract produced winners. The
 question this project asks is whether those wins are
 reproducible, and what the data says is that they
 are not, at current entry prices, without fundamental
 structural change.

 Five Americas
 
 The national data tells one story. Five American
 communities tell five others, each shaped by a

 Six Decades of Economic Divergence
 What national averages conceal

 The national Dream Index describes an average, but
 averages conceal as much as they reveal. To understand
 how the asset contract operates in practice, this project
 examines five communities whose economic trajectories have
 diverged sharply from national benchmarks since 1960.
 Each place was chosen because it embodies a distinct
 structural mechanism: racial exclusion from the original
 postwar architecture, extraction economy collapse,
 manufacturing displacement, colonial land dispossession,
 and concentrated asset-economy gains.
 

 
 
 
 Sharecropper plowing, Montgomery County, Alabama, c. 1937.
 In Sunflower County, Mississippi in 1960, 74% of residents
 lived below the poverty line. The GI Bill and FHA were
 administered locally, by the same institutions that
 enforced segregation.

 The three metrics, median income relative to national,
 poverty rate, and homeownership rate, are measured at each
 decennial census from 1960 to 2020 using county-level data
 from the National Historical Geographic Information System
 (NHGIS). What you are looking at is not natural variation.
 It is the geography of policy decisions made between 1944
 and 2000 whose consequences are still compounding.
 
 





 
 
 
 Five Mechanisms
 
 
 Five mechanisms. One contract.
 

 
 
 
 Mississippi Delta
 Excluded by design since Reconstruction
 The original exclusion. Sixty years of compounded returns
 on an asset you were prevented from buying is the racial
 wealth gap.
 
 

 
 
 
 Coal Country
 Extraction economy abandoned after the asset ran out
 When the coal ran out, the company left and took the
 infrastructure with it. The opioid crisis is the final
 chapter of economic abandonment.
 
 

 
 
 
 Rust Belt
 Manufacturing made disposable by globalization
 The plant was a social contract. When it closed, the
 contract ended overnight.
 
 

 
 
 
 Pine Ridge
 Never inside the Dream, the colonial baseline
 Not a place where the Dream failed. A place the Dream
 never reached. The poverty rate has never fallen below 35%.
 
 

 
 
 
 Bay Area / NYC
 What winning the asset economy looks like
 The inverse. Even a median income at 1.5× the national
 average cannot afford the local housing market. The Dream
 is broken here too, in the opposite direction.

 Income vs. Wealth
 The gap that income policy cannot close

 The racial income gap has narrowed by six percentage
 points in 57 years. That is real progress. But the racial
 wealth gap, the difference in what households own, not
 what they earn, has barely moved. Black households held
 9.3 cents of wealth for every dollar held by white
 households in 1989. Today they hold 12 cents.
 

 
 
 
 Home Owners' Loan Corporation security map, Brooklyn, late
 1930s. Red zones, majority-Black neighborhoods, were
 systematically denied FHA mortgage insurance. This single
 policy instrument created the wealth gap that persists today.
 Wikimedia Commons. Public domain.
 
 

 
 This is the asset contract's central evidence. Income
 and wages move together when the economy grows. Wealth
 compounds independently of current income, it accumulates
 from assets bought decades ago, from inheritances, from
 equity in homes purchased before prices ran away. A policy
 that addresses only wages addresses only half the mechanism.
 The other half is the asset itself: who owns it, who was
 prevented from owning it, and how many decades of
 compounding that prevention represents.

 These five communities did not experience what came

 2000, 2015
 The Crossing
 
 In 2011, for the first time in American history,
 the cost of a canonical middle-class life exceeded
 the median household income.
 
 
 The Dream Index crossed 1.0. The math that had been
 tilting for thirty years finally broke through.
 
 
 
 "Inside America's Capital of Despair: Youngstown", YouTube
 
 





 
 
 
 The Inflection
 
 
 When the math finally broke
 

 The financial crisis of 2008 dropped
 median incomes while healthcare and education costs kept
 rising. By 2011, the accumulated weight of thirty years
 of divergence reached the tipping point.

 Low interest rates between 2012 and
 2020 created a temporary window, falling mortgage
 payments made housing affordable despite rising prices.
 Americans who bought in that window got the last
 affordable entry point. In 2022, rates doubled. The
 window closed permanently.

 
 "The rate floor was a reprieve, not a recovery.
 The Dream Index has not returned below 1.0."

 What It Cost
 
 The economic pressure did not stay in balance sheets.
 It showed up in bedrooms, birth certificates,
 and obituaries.
 
 
 
 "A Thunder-Being Nation: The Oglala Lakota of Pine Ridge", YouTube
 
 





 
 
 
 The Consequences
 
 
 Economic statistics are human statistics
 

 Median age at first marriage rose by
 six years since 1960. Americans say in surveys they want
 more children than they have, they cite cost as the
 reason. The U.S. is the only wealthy country where life
 expectancy declined after 2014.

 
 "The country is paying its bills in lifespans
 and childlessness."
 

 Working-age Americans without college
 degrees started dying earlier in the 2000s from suicide,
 overdose, and alcohol. These deaths map almost precisely
 onto the geography of economic abandonment shown in the
 Five Americas data.
 





 
 The Price Paid in Years and Choices
 Economic distress does not stay in financial statements

 When households cannot afford the basket of basic life,
 they respond rationally, by restructuring the shape of
 their lives. They delay marriage because forming a household
 requires two incomes and a deposit they cannot save. They
 have fewer children than they say they want because childcare
 costs more than rent in most American cities. They move back
 in with parents because renting alone consumes more than 30%
 of take-home income. And in communities where economic
 abandonment is most complete, they die younger.

 The four indicators below, median age at first marriage,
 total fertility rate, share of adults in multigenerational
 households, and life expectancy at birth, are not separate
 phenomena. They are four different measurements of the same
 underlying pressure. Each has moved in the direction the
 Dream Index would predict, and each movement accelerated
 after 2000, when the index began its final climb toward 1.0.

 This is what the data looks like when you measure it
 not in dollars, but in years of life and choices foreclosed.

 Recommendations
 
 
 What the evidence demands
 

 Federal policymakers
 should fund universal asset-building accounts at birth
 because our analysis found the racial wealth gap has
 barely closed in six decades despite narrowing income
 gaps, wealth cannot be addressed through wage policy alone.
 

 State legislators
 should preempt restrictive zoning because our analysis
 found housing costs have outpaced wages in every metro
 area since 1990, with supply constraint as the primary
 structural driver.

 Congress should restore
 the GI Bill as an asset-transfer program because our
 analysis found contemporary veterans' wealth outcomes
 diverge from WWII-era veterans specifically where the
 original GI Bill provided asset access.

 
 "The architecture of the Dream was built through
 specific decisions. Rebuilding it requires specific
 decisions, not generic growth, but targeted
 structural repair."
 
 





 
 What This Project Found
 Seven findings. One story.

 The evidence assembled across this project points to
 a single structural shift: the American economy transitioned,
 between roughly 1973 and 2011, from a system that delivered
 middle-class life through wages to one that requires asset
 ownership, credentialed employment, or inherited capital.
 The seven findings below are not separate arguments. They
 are seven different measurements of the same underlying change,
 each confirming it from a distinct angle, the basket, the
 labor market, the racial wealth gap, the geography of
 abandonment, and the shape of American lives.

 Methodology
 
 
 Technical Documentation
 Methodology & Data
 

 The Dream Index measures
 the cost of housing, healthcare, education, childcare,
 transportation, and food as a multiple of median household
 income. All values in real 2024 dollars using CPI-U as
 the deflator. Primary healthcare measure uses the full
 KFF family premium (crosses 1.0 in 2011). Conservative
 lower bound uses household exposure only (crosses 2022).

 Data sources:
 FRED (38 series), KFF Employer Health Benefits Survey
 (1999–2024), NCES Digest Table 330.10 (1963+), NHGIS
 county-level census data (1960–2020), CDC NCHS life
 expectancy and birth rates, BLS Consumer Price Indices.

 Five places:
 Counties aggregated to place level using population-weighted
 averages. Pine Ridge merges FIPS 46-102 and 46-113 as one
 continuous series. All income comparisons use nominal
 values divided by national nominal median, the ratio
 cancels inflation, no deflation required.

 
 Full methodology, sensitivity analyses, and data files:
 dream_index_metadata.json
